To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Bentley beam algorithm, using fixed beams summed at 10° intervals, is accurate within 2% in the treatment volume for an 18 MV x-ray beam and a 7.2 cm × 7.2cm field size.

the Bentley beam algorithm, with fixed beam data summed at 10° angular steps, predicts dose in the treatment region with accuracy of about 2% and dose at depths between surface and treatment region with accuracy as high as 10%.

(a) angular step size and extent of beam profiles are important factors that influence the accuracy of rotational x‐ray dose calculations; (b) the angular step size should be less than 5° for summation of stored beam profiles; and (c) beam profiles should extend 4 cm outside of the edge of the treatment field.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an algorithm for rotational therapy dose calculation based on the Bentley model.
the development of a computer program to calculate the dose distributions for a rotational therapy beam.
the development of a computer algorithm to predict the dose distributions for rotational therapy beams using the Bentley beam model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

for the 180° arc and field size used in this study, the dose in the center of the treatment volume can be calculated with a precision of 2% by using the Bentley beam model with fixed beams summed at 10° intervals.
the accuracy of the dose distribution calculation is directly related to the extent of the beam data and the number of fixed beams used in the summation algorithm.

the Bentley beam profile data, when used in the algorithm described, can predict the dose distribution to within 2% in the treatment volume and within 5% for depths between the surface and treatment volume.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of a finite angular step and a finite profile extent in the calculation of rotational dose distribution can result in significant errors, particularly at shallow depths.
the Bentley beam data are adequate for most clinical situations, but for those cases where increased accuracy is required, the beam profiles must be extended and angular steps reduced.
the accuracy of the rotational x‐ray dose calculation depends on the extent of the beam profile and the angular step of the fixed beam summation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the accuracy of rotational x‐ray dose distributions depends on the extent of profile data used in the calculations, as well as the angular steps for summation of the fixed beams.
the angular step size used in rotational dose calculation algorithms can have an impact on accuracy.
, for rotational therapy beams with finite angular steps, dose calculations are most accurate at the isocenter of the treatment volume.
